lines.say: Here's a puzzle. A box hides a secret string of bits, like one zero one.
Picture a wall of switches, some secretly wired to a buzzer.
The buzzer only says whether an odd or an even number of wired switches are on.
Normally you test one switch at a time, so three switches take three questions, and a hundred take a hundred.
A quantum computer needs just one question.
Each switch gets its own qubit, a quantum bit, set by an H gate to a state called plus.
One extra answer qubit is set to minus. Then we ask the box, once.
Each wired switch kicks a minus sign, called a phase, back onto its own qubit, turning plus into minus.
Measure now, and plus and minus look the same, half and half. The secret hides in the signs.
So one more H on each qubit turns plus back into zero, and minus into one.
Measure, and we read one zero one. The whole secret, from a single question.
This isn't the computer quietly trying every input and collecting answers.
It asks once, and interference, where possibilities add or cancel like ripples, leaves the secret as the only possible reading.
Here's where the switch wall breaks. No real panel can be tested all at once like this.
It only works because the hidden rule is odd or even, a parity, which interference can unpick. Most rules aren't.
So that's Bernstein Vazirani. Phase kickback on every input at once, and one question reveals the whole secret string.
